transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-06-11
- Time: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Acme, Lead ML Eng), Sofia Kim (Acme, Platform Eng), Nina Patel (Acme, CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood and Acme AI Labs ran a technical deep dive on throughput tuning for the Redwood inference runtime. Focus areas: continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Action items include sharing scheduler config examples, customer sending token distribution traces, and scheduling a follow-up benchmark.

Topics: continuous batching; scheduler parameters and knobs; max_num_seqs vs latency; token length limits and tail latencies; KV cache warmup and eviction; quantization impact on throughput; VPC/on-prem networking impacts on latency.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account.
[00:05] Carlos Mendez: Hi, Carlos here. We have Sofia and Nina on the line as well. Thanks for doing this.
[00:09] Priya Rao: Hi, Priya from Redwood SE — I'll drive the technical bits. Quick note: we'll talk continuous batching and some scheduler knobs, but if at any time you want deep kernel-level stuff I can follow up.
[00:18] Nina Patel: Great, thanks. We're particularly worried about throughput for our chat product, we see big spikes in token generation per request and tail latency is killing user experience.
[00:27] Jordan Lee: Understood. Can you confirm current deployment mode — hosted or VPC/dedicated?
[00:31] Sofia Kim: We're on a hybrid right now — mostly hosted for dev, and evaluating Dedicated (or on-prem) for production. We need predictable throughput and data residency.
[00:40] Priya Rao: Perfect. For throughput tuning we usually look at three layers: request scheduling (continuous batching), runtime knobs like max_num_seqs and max_tokens_per_batch, and model execution knobs (quantization, kernel selection). Also KV cache behavior for chat workloads.
[00:52] Carlos Mendez: Quick question: what's the tradeoff if we raise max_num_seqs? We want higher throughput but not to blow up p50 latency.
[00:58] Priya Rao: Good question. Increasing max_num_seqs allows more concurrent sequences to be packed in a micro-batch, which improves GPU utilization and throughput. But it also increases the time a request may wait in queue to reach that pack size — so tail latency can increase if arrival rates are bursty.
[01:13] Priya Rao: Our scheduler has adaptive windowing: it targets target_batch_fill and max_wait_ms. If you set max_num_seqs too high and max_wait_ms too large, you'll see improved throughput but higher p95/p99. If you want lower tails, reduce max_wait_ms or enable partial flush thresholds.
[01:29] Sofia Kim: What's partial flush?
[01:31] Priya Rao: Partial flush is where the scheduler will send a smaller-than-full batch if the oldest request has been waiting longer than a threshold. That keeps tails bounded while still capturing some batching benefit.
[01:40] Carlos Mendez: Makes sense. We have a token distribution that is heavy-tailed — median length is 30 tokens but 10% are >512. How does that affect batching?
[01:49] Priya Rao: Long sequences complicate batching — they increase GPU active time per sequence and reduce effective packing. Two strategies: 1) set a token limit per batch (max_total_tokens) to avoid long sequences dominating a micro-batch; 2) use length-based routing — put long requests on a different queue or model variant. Also consider KV cache warmup and memory fragmentation for long seqs.
[02:06] Jordan Lee: For length-based routing we can create a 'long-seq' route that hits a model with a different batch profile or higher memory. That can be automated in policy routing.
[02:14] Nina Patel: Any quantization impact here? We plan to run int8 for cost reasons.
[02:17] Priya Rao: Quantization helps throughput and memory. For int8 you usually get 1.5-2x token throughput improvement depending on kernel and model architecture. Downside: sometimes slightly reduced sample quality or higher variance in decoding time per token. Also some kernels behave differently with long sequences — check KV cache memory layout. We recommend running small A/B evals on your prompt set.
[02:35] Carlos Mendez: We're also testing continuous batching — is it equivalent to our current 'micro-batching' approach?
[02:40] Priya Rao: Continuous batching in Redwood is a scheduler mode that constantly aggregates incoming requests into micro-batches with very low latency constraints. It has parameters like target_batch_fill, max_num_seqs, max_wait_ms, max_total_tokens. Micro-batching is a concept; continuous batching is an implementation we tune for steady-state high QPS.
[02:57] Sofia Kim: We saw jitter in latency during burst tests. Could that be network (VPC) or scheduler?
[03:03] Priya Rao: Could be both. On VPC/on-prem you add network hops, gRPC retransmits, and NAT timeouts — that can add jitter. Also scheduler windows reacting to bursty traffic can cause micro-batch fill variability. We typically recommend pinning instances (no autoscaling) for benchmark runs to isolate network effects.
[03:20] Jordan Lee: Also share that our Dedicated nodes support colocated networking to reduce cross-host hops; for on-prem the team can help install a tuned network path.
[03:27] Carlos Mendez: Good. About KV cache: we get a lot of repeated prefixes across users in the chat. How does the runtime optimize prefix caching?
[03:34] Priya Rao: We have prefix/KV cache that stores common KV states per model + prompt fingerprint. For chat workloads, a prefix cache hit bypasses recomputing the KV for the prefix which dramatically reduces token compute for the next tokens. But eviction policy and TTL matter — if your user base has lots of unique prefixes, hit rate drops. We can instrument cache hit rates per route to see benefits.
[03:51] Sofia Kim: Are there knobs for cache TTL or shard size?
[03:54] Priya Rao: Yes, we expose TTL, max_entries, and shard_count. TTL controls how long a prefix is kept; lower TTL reduces memory usage but drops hits. Shard_count influences concurrency and eviction granularity. For high QPS chat, we increase max_entries and tune TTL to observed reuse intervals.
[04:10] Nina Patel: Does quantization affect cache correctness?
[04:12] Priya Rao: Not correctness — the KV cache stores activations. Quantized kernels may store compressed representations but logically it's consistent. However, due to numerical differences you might see slightly different logits which affects sampling. It's minor but worth evaluating.
[04:24] Carlos Mendez: We have one more thing: scheduler knobs — can you walk through priority knobs and a recommended starting config for our workload (median short, tail long)?
[04:33] Priya Rao: Sure — recommended starting config for mixed short+long:
- target_batch_fill: 64 sequences (or lower depending on GPU memory)
- max_num_seqs: 128 (allows growth but don't exceed if you want bounded tails)
- max_wait_ms: 8-12ms for low p50, raise to 25-40ms if you want higher throughput and can tolerate p95 increase
- partial_flush_threshold: 0.25 (flush when 25% filled if oldest request is older than threshold_ms)
- max_total_tokens: set to something like 8192 tokens per micro-batch to prevent long seq hogging

[05:03] Priya Rao: Also enable length-based queues: short-queue and long-queue. Route >256 tokens to long-queue which has max_num_seqs smaller but higher mem per seq.
[05:13] Carlos Mendez: That'll help. On the hardware side, what are good GPU configs? We currently have A10Gs and are considering A100s.
[05:20] Priya Rao: A100 gives better fp16 and int8 throughput and larger memory for KV. A10 is cost-effective but you'll be more constrained on max_num_seqs for long seqs. For Dedicated we can size pools: e.g., 8xA10 or 4xA100 depending on concurrency. We can run head-to-head benchmarks.
[05:33] Sofia Kim: Can we get a sample benchmark config to run locally?
[05:36] Priya Rao: Yes — I'll share a scheduler knobs doc with example YML, a load profile generator script, and instructions to pin CPUs and disable autoscaling. Also include prometheus metrics to export: batch_fill, queue_wait_ms, kv_cache_hit_rate, gpu_utilization, per-token latency.
[05:49] Jordan Lee: We'll attach those docs and sample configs as follow-up. Carlos, if you can send token histograms and traces we can simulate your mix.
[05:56] Carlos Mendez: Sure, we'll export traces from our gateway — expect that by end of week.
[05:59] Nina Patel: One more question: if we go on-prem, are there limitations on scheduler knobs or KV cache?
[06:05] Priya Rao: Functionally not — the runtime is the same. The main differences are network topology and hardware procurement. On-prem customers need to ensure RDMA or high-bandwidth interconnects for multi-host KV sharing if you plan to scale horizontally. For single-host Dedicated it's straightforward.
[06:18] Sofia Kim: Anything else about token limits? We saw an error where requests >1024 tokens were rejected in dev.
[06:24] Priya Rao: That sounds like an API-level limit on your hosted environment. There are two places for limits: API/ingress (we enforce a per-request max_tokens) and runtime per-model sequence length. We'll check both. In Dedicated you can raise ingress limits aligned with model max_seq.
[06:36] Carlos Mendez: Ok, that explains earlier failures.
[06:39] Jordan Lee: Quick recap of action items: Priya shares scheduler knobs + sample configs; Carlos to send traces and token distribution; Jordan to send Dedicated pricing and capacity options; schedule benchmark on 6/18.
[06:51] Sofia Kim: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[06:54] Nina Patel: Thanks.
[06:55] Priya Rao: Thanks — I'll follow up with the doc links and a checklist for the benchmark run.
[07:00] Jordan Lee: Meeting adjourned.
